newsitem.title: UK: Global dash for gas set to sweep Asia.
newsitem.headline: Global dash for gas set to sweep Asia.

text.p: Asia's booming economies may be heading for a greener future if several multi-billion dollar pipeline projects aimed at supplying "clean" power-provider natural gas come to fruition.
But analysts warn that the region will have to wait for huge projects to bring gas from Russia and Central Asia.
The attraction of gas for Asia is that it is both plentiful and clean, said analyst Stephen O'Sullivan of MC Securities in London.
This means it is well placed both to meet new energy demand, and to displace coal with all its associated pollution problems in the existing market.
"There are large changes in consumption patterns in the region" he said, "for example in South Korea, where they are switching from coal. China is potentially a very big market."

He added that globally, gas is outperforming general energy growth because of growing environmental pressure. While this is still not as important an issue as in Europe, it is becoming more of a concern in Asia.
The growth of gas use around the world has been spectacular.
In the last ten years global demand has risen by a third and consumption is around 60 percent of that of its big brother, oil.
The Asia Pacific region already contributes to this, with gas use increasing by 7.5 percent in 1996 over the previous year to 235 billion cubic metres (bcm).
Most of this is liquefied natural gas produced within the region in Malaysia, Indonesia or Australia, or shipped from the Middle East.
But consumption could change out of recognition if plans to move natural gas by pipeline from the giant fields of Russia and the central Asian republic of Turkmenistan go ahead.
O'Sullivan pointed out that Russia's supplies are so large it cannot sell all the gas it needs to in its traditional markets in Europe.
"Russia...will also have to look at Asia. An awful lot might be used in China, both to displace coal and to satisfy booming energy demand," he said.
The chairman of the world's largest gas company Russia's Gazprom, Rem Vyakhirev, recently announced his company's intention of targeting Asia.
Russia plans to develop gas fields in Irkutsk and Yakutia in Siberia and to link Siberian fields by pipeline with China, North and South Korea and "very likely" Japan.
"We are aware that gas from the Middle East may start competing with Russian gas in the region in the next 10 to 15 years," he said. "But Gazprom expects the Russian gas to win the competition."
And senior officials from Turkmenistan and Japan recently reiterated plans to build a pipeline from the Turkmen gas fields to the Pacific and also eventually on to Japan.

"If Turkmenistan's natural resources reach the Pacific Ocean and the pipeline goes as far as Japan, there is no doubt this will have a positive effect on peace and stability in the Asian region," Keizo Obuchi, special councillor to the Japanese Prime Minister, said earlier this month.

There are also other plans to build major pipelines from Turkmenistan through Afghanistan to Pakistan and India, as well as smaller scale projects, like a pipeline from Burma to Thailand already underway.
The vice President of the Japan Gas Association, Koshiro Goda, told a conference in June that East Asian demand will double from 140 bcm a year now to around 300 bcm a year by 2010.

"On the one hand its utilisation as an electric power generation fuel is expected to rise," he said. "On the other hand, its employment in the manufacture of chemicals and fertilisers as well as a fuel for industrial purposes is anticipated to burgeon."
But Jonathan Stern, senior vice president at analyst Gas Strategies sounded a note of warning over the pace of growth.

"The projects (Gazprom's) Vyakhirev was talking about are fascinating, but he was talking about a timeframe of 2010. So yes, it's very exciting, but not immediate," he said, adding that there were many political, economic and financial issues to sort out before these projects become reality.

He believed the only major pipeline project with a chance of getting off the ground in the near term was the trans-Afghanistan link to Pakistan, but "only if the country becomes more stable than it has been in the last 20 years."
Otherwise, Stern said "the Turkmens are desperate to find markets for their gas anywhere, and the Russians are interested in Asia but they're not in a hurry."
